summary: The Kodiaq Select Plug-in Hybrid is the only plug-in grade in Skoda Australia's large-SUV range, and its 19.7kWh usable battery and 110km WLTP electric range put it within a few kilometres of its VW Tiguan and Tayron eHybrid platform-mates and well clear of the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV — enough that a Melbourne commuter with home charging would rarely wake the 1.5-litre engine. Reviewers are near-unanimous that the drivetrain is smooth and the cabin genuinely large, and equally unanimous on the catch: this is the one Kodiaq you cannot have with seven seats or all-wheel drive, because the battery sits where the third row goes. Where they split is value — CarExpert notes the $8,500 premium over the petrol Select 4x4 buys you fewer seats and less traction, while Chasing Cars still calls it easy to recommend against a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV or BYD Sealion 6.
pros: 110km of WLTP electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery sits just below the 113-117km of the VW Tiguan and Tayron eHybrids on the same powertrain and comfortably beats the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 83-86km and the Kia Sorento PHEV's 55km
50kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in 25 minutes) plus 11kW AC is unusual on a plug-in hybrid; neither the Outlander PHEV nor the Sealion 6 can take DC at all

Seven-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty applies with no strings — Skoda Australia made it standard across the range in September 2022 and it is not tied to buying a service pack or servicing inside the dealer network; the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km
745 litres behind the second row and 1,945 litres with it folded is more usable space than most five-seat rivals, and the second row slides and reclines
At $63,490 before on-roads it sits below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold, and at 42g/km CO2 it clears Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car test, so stamp duty is charged at the flat green rate
cons: Five seats only — the battery occupies the third-row well, so the one Kodiaq a large family would most want is the one that cannot carry seven; the petrol Select, Sportline and RS all seat seven and even the cheaper mild-hybrid offers a seven-seat option for $2,000

The 1.9L/100km label figure only holds if you plug in every night: with the battery flat, the same car on 19-inch wheels is rated at 5.9L/100km on WLTP (ADAC), and Chasing Cars managed about 800km from a full battery and 45-litre tank on an interstate run, so the economics collapse for a buyer who cannot charge at home
Front-wheel drive only and 1,800kg braked towing, against 4x4 and 2,300kg on every petrol Kodiaq — CarExpert lists 'loses all-wheel drive' among its three headline dislikes

No spare wheel: the PHEV gets a tyre inflation kit where every other Kodiaq gets a space-saver, it loses the 289-litre third-row boot area, and the head-up display is only available in the $6,500 Signature Package

Plug-in hybrids lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and Skoda Australia is already advertising the car at $59,990 drive-away against a $68,990 launch drive-away published in its own April 2026 spec sheet — roughly $9,000 off within months of launch, which is a real resale-value warning
